opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, what struck me most was how he thinks about a problem before he touches any code. Back then I was an intern, and like most young researchers I wanted to try many things fast: add a module, tweak a loss, run it and see. Kaiming works almost the opposite way. He keeps asking what the real bottleneck is, and he wants to strip everything down until the core question is very clean.

During the ImageNet work there was a lot of pressure. It's a competition, there's a deadline, and it's tempting to stack tricks to squeeze out a bit more accuracy. But Kaiming always looked for the simple idea underneath. If something worked, he wanted to know why. If you couldn't explain it in one or two sentences, he didn't really trust it. That's part of why his work tends to last. ResNet is an extremely simple idea, but it came from a very clear understanding of what was going wrong with optimizing deep networks.

The other thing is his patience and his taste for experiments. He designs experiments almost like a scientist in a lab. Each run is supposed to answer one specific question, not just produce a number. He'd look at training curves very carefully and notice small things that other people would skip. Many of his ideas come from that kind of careful observation, not from some sudden inspiration.

He's also very honest with himself. If an idea doesn't hold up, he lets it go, even if he's spent a lot of time on it. As a young person, watching that up close changed how I think about research. Being clever isn't the main thing. What matters is being clear, being simple, and being really honest about what the results are telling you. I've tried to carry that into my own work and into how I mentor students now.

r001.rationale: The response describes Kaiming finding a simple idea beneath a problem and turning it into lasting work, using ResNet as an example of a simple idea grounded in a clear understanding of deep-network optimization.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the thing that stood out most was his sense of taste, and how disciplined he was about it. At the time I was still fairly junior, and my instinct was to try lots of things and see what moved the number. Kaiming was almost the opposite. Before touching any experiment he would spend a long time just asking, "What is the real problem here? Why does this fail?" He wanted a clean story about the phenomenon first, and only then would he design the experiments to test it.

The other thing was how much he valued simplicity. There were many moments where we had something that worked but had five moving parts, and he would keep pushing to strip it down. If a component wasn't necessary to explain the result, it had to go. He had this conviction that if an idea is right, it should be expressible in a very simple way, and if you can't make it simple, you probably don't understand it yet. That's not a comfortable process, because you're often throwing away things that gave you a gain, but it's why his work tends to age so well.

And he was very grounded in experiments. He didn't trust intuition alone, and he didn't trust a single number either. He'd want to see the trend across model sizes, across datasets, in ablations, until the picture was consistent everywhere. Working with him taught me that a research idea isn't finished when it works, it's finished when you can explain in one sentence why it works. That mindset shaped how I approach research to this day.

r001.rationale: The response describes Kaiming’s taste, simplicity, and experimental discipline, but does not communicate that he could turn seemingly ordinary ideas into valuable research ideas.

astra-6.text:
What stood out to me was his ability to get to the core of a problem. With something like the ImageNet Challenge, it’s easy to focus on making the score a little better. But he would step back and ask, “What is actually making this difficult? Is there a simpler way to think about it?”

And then he was very disciplined about testing that intuition. Having an elegant idea is one thing; designing an experiment that tells you whether the idea is right is another. That combination—asking a fundamental question and then being very concrete about how to investigate it—was what impressed me.

r001.rationale: The response describes identifying a problem’s core and testing a fundamental idea, but does not communicate that Kaiming turns seemingly ordinary ideas into valuable research ideas.

sol-6.1.text:
What stood out to me was how deeply he would think about a very simple question. In the ImageNet Challenge, there’s a temptation to keep adding things—another trick, another component—to improve the number. Kaiming would step back and ask, “What is the actual problem here? Why should this work?”

And he was very good at turning that question into a clean experiment. An idea didn’t have to sound complicated or impressive. It had to reveal something. Working with him helped me appreciate that the hard part of research is often finding the right question and stripping away everything that makes the answer harder to see.

r001.rationale: The response describes Kaiming’s distinctive approach of starting with a simple question and shaping it into a clean experiment that reveals something, conveying how ordinary ideas became valuable research.
